prompt: Quitanda's export job writes `raw/orders/01-10-2026/orders.csv`, `raw/orders/02-10-2026/orders.csv` and so on. What goes wrong when somebody lists `raw/orders/` at the end of the year?

choices.text: Cloud Storage refuses the hyphens inside an object's name
choices.why: An object name may hold almost any UTF-8 up to 1,024 bytes; hyphens are fine.

choices.text: Each month's first day lists together, as names sort by bytes
choices.why: Right: the listing is lexicographic, and a day-month-year date puts the 01s of every month side by side.

choices.text: The folders are created out of order and some of them end up empty
choices.why: There are no folders to create: a prefix exists only while some object's name starts with it.

choices.text: Nothing; Cloud Storage lists objects in the order they were written
choices.why: It lists in the order of the names' bytes, not of their creation.

prompt: A colleague deletes the only object under `raw/tmp/` in a bucket without hierarchical namespace. What does `gcloud storage ls gs://quitanda-raw-dev/raw/` show afterwards?

choices.why: That is a file system's habit; a flat namespace has nothing left to remove.

choices.text: An error
choices.why: Listing a prefix nothing starts with is an ordinary, empty answer.

choices.text: `raw/tmp/` for seven days, the soft-delete window
choices.why: Soft delete keeps the deleted object's bytes, not a folder in the listing.

choices.text: No `raw/tmp/` at all
choices.why: Right: a folder exists only while some object's name starts with it.

prompt: Match each storage class to its minimum stay.

choices.text: In Standard, unmanaged and paying no management fee
choices.why: Right: objects smaller than 128 KiB are not managed and not counted.

prompt: An administrator of the project wants the invoice bucket protected against a colleague who means to delete invoices. Which setting does it?

choices.why: Whoever may delete a live object may also delete its generations.

choices.text: A retention policy left unlocked, so it can still be adjusted
choices.why: Anybody who may change the bucket may clear an unlocked policy first.

choices.text: Soft delete set to its longest duration of 90 days
choices.why: Soft delete undoes accidents; it is no defence against somebody who means it.

choices.text: A retention policy that is then locked
choices.why: Right: a locked policy cannot be removed by anybody, the project's owner included.

prompt: A bucket's IAM policy grants `roles/storage.objectViewer` to `allUsers`, and nobody can find out who added it. Public access prevention is then set to `enforced`. What happens to the grant?

choices.why: The grant is left where it is; it simply stops working.

choices.text: It stays written in the policy and grants nothing

choices.text: The setting is refused until the grant is removed by hand

choices.text: It keeps working for objects written before the change
choices.why: Prevention applies to every object of the bucket, old and new.

prompt: On a regional Cloud SQL instance, a migration runs `DELETE FROM orders` without a `WHERE`. What does high availability do about it?

choices.text: It keeps the deleted rows for seven days on the standby
choices.why: That is point-in-time recovery's log, and it restores into a new instance.

choices.text: It refuses the statement
choices.why: The primary takes every write; the standby takes no connections at all.

choices.text: Nothing; the standby holds the same delete

prompt: Somebody wants Tuesday's backup back and runs `gcloud sql backups restore BACKUP_ID --restore-instance=quitanda-orders` on the production instance. What happens to the orders written since Tuesday?

choices.why: Right: restore into another instance first, look, then decide.

choices.text: They are kept, as a restore creates a new instance beside the old one
choices.why: That is point-in-time recovery; restoring a backup does not.

choices.why: A backup is a disk at one moment; nothing merges it with what came after.

choices.why: A replica replays the primary; it is neither a backup nor a standby.

prompt: A customer places an order, and the next page reads it back from a read replica. What may the customer see?

choices.text: The order, since Cloud SQL replicas are synchronous
choices.why: They are asynchronous: the primary commits, answers, and only then sends the change.

choices.text: That the order does not exist, if the replica has not replayed it yet
choices.why: Right: reads that must see their own writes belong on the primary.

choices.text: A duplicate order, written once on each server
choices.why: A replica refuses writes; there is only one place the order was written.

prompt: Quitanda's reports ask about days, weeks and months, and one dashboard asks about the evening rush. Why not partition the orders by hour?

choices.text: Wide queries open sixteen times the files
choices.why: Right: partition by the coarsest unit the common filters still prune well; cluster for the hour.

choices.text: BigQuery has no hourly partitioning
choices.why: Time partitions can be hourly; the cost is elsewhere.

choices.text: An hourly partition is billed a 10 MB minimum of its own
choices.why: The minimum is per table referenced and per query, not per partition.

choices.text: The hour is not a column the dashboards could filter on
choices.why: It could be; the point is what the finer cut costs every other query.

prompt: A query processes 25,000,000 bytes. BigQuery rounds a query up to the next MB of 1,048,576 bytes. How many bytes is it billed?
A DuckDB plan is read from the ___, where the table is read, up to the top, where the answer leaves.
September's sales per district select `district` and `total_cents` and name `dt` only in the `WHERE`. Is `dt` part of the bytes billed?

choices.text: No, because a filter column is not returned
choices.why: Billing follows what is read, and the filter has to read it.

choices.text: Yes, 8 bytes a row over the days the filter keeps
choices.why: Right: every column referenced counts, wherever it is referenced.

choices.text: No, because the partitioning column is free on demand
choices.why: It costs nothing on disk in those Parquet files, and its full width on the bill.

choices.text: Only for the days the filter rules out
choices.why: It is the other way round: the days kept are the ones read.

prompt: In BigQuery's execution graph, one stage shows a maximum compute time far above its average. What does that point to?

choices.text: Slot contention, the query waiting for slots
choices.why: That shows as a long wait with little read or compute.

choices.text: A larger bill, since slow stages read more bytes
choices.why: On demand the bill was fixed before the graph existed, by columns and partitions.

choices.text: Shuffle spilling to disk for lack of memory
choices.why: Spill is reported as its own figure, shuffle bytes spilled.

choices.text: Skew: one worker got far more than the rest
choices.why: Right: the stage ends when its slowest worker does.

prompt: An analyst should query the order files in a bucket through BigQuery, and must not read the bucket with any other tool. What makes that possible?

choices.text: A plain external table, with read access to the bucket
choices.why: That grants her the bucket, every file in it, through any tool.

choices.text: An object table over the bucket
choices.why: An object table lists metadata, one row per object, not the orders' rows.

choices.text: A BigLake table, over a connection
choices.why: Right: BigQuery reads the files on her behalf, so she needs no permission on the bucket.

choices.text: Public access prevention on the bucket
choices.why: That stops `allUsers` grants; it gives BigQuery nothing to read through.

prompt: A BigLake table caches its metadata with `max_staleness` of four hours. A new day's file lands at 09:00. What may a query at 09:30 that uses the cache see?

choices.text: The new file, since a write invalidates the cache
choices.why: A write to the bucket tells BigQuery nothing; staleness is what is allowed.

choices.text: The table without the new file
choices.why: Right: the price of the cache is that the table may be behind the bucket.

choices.text: An error, until a refresh
choices.why: Within the staleness the cache is trusted, and the query runs.

choices.text: Half the new file, the row groups already listed
choices.why: The cache holds files and their footers; a file is in it or not.

prompt: Quitanda leaves the order files in the bucket and queries them as an external table. What does that give up against a native table?

choices.text: Partition pruning, which needs data inside BigQuery
choices.why: Hive-style `dt=` folders are read as a partition column by an external table too.

choices.text: On-demand billing
choices.why: On demand bills an external query per TiB like any other.

choices.text: A single copy of the data, since the files are loaded too
choices.why: The files ARE the table; nothing is stored twice.

choices.text: Clustering, and the long-term rate
choices.why: Right: BigQuery does not arrange the files, and they are billed as Cloud Storage objects.

prompt: BI Engine in `southamerica-east1` costs 0.0749 USD per GiB-hour. What does a 5 GiB reservation cost in a 730-hour month, in USD to the cent?
A dashboard query asks for something `daily_sales_mv` cannot answer, so smart tuning cannot rewrite it. What happens?

choices.text: It runs against the base table and is billed as such, with no warning
choices.why: Right: there is no error and no line on the bill; it just costs what it would have.

choices.text: It fails, with a message naming the view
choices.why: Nothing fails; that is why the fallback goes unnoticed.

choices.text: BigQuery refreshes the view so it can answer
choices.why: A refresh catches the view up; it does not change what it can answer.

choices.text: It reads the view and returns the closest rows it has
choices.why: A rewrite happens only when everything the query needs is in the view.

prompt: Quitanda wants the median order value per district for each day, kept ready for the morning. Why a scheduled query rather than a materialised view?

choices.text: A materialised view cannot be partitioned by `dt`
choices.why: The lesson's view is partitioned on the same column as its base table.

choices.text: A scheduled query is free, while a view's refresh is billed
choices.why: A scheduled query is billed as the query it runs.

choices.text: A median cannot be maintained by combining stored parts with new rows
choices.why: Right: two days' medians do not make the median of both, so it is recomputed on a timetable.

choices.text: Materialised views refresh only once a week
choices.why: They refresh after the base table changes, no more often than the interval set.

prompt: On demand, BI Engine accelerates a dashboard query. What is the stage that reads the table data billed?

choices.text: The usual bytes, at a discounted rate
choices.why: The pricing page says those stages are charged for 0 scanned bytes.

choices.text: The 10 MB minimum
choices.why: The accelerated stage is charged nothing at all.

choices.text: Zero scanned bytes
choices.why: Right: the stage BI Engine serves is free; the memory is paid as a reservation.

choices.text: The slots the stage used, at the Standard edition's price
choices.why: On demand there are no slot-hours to bill.

prompt: A Pub/Sub subscription filter can select messages by their ___ alone, since Pub/Sub never parses the `data` of a message.
Which of these did the Pub/Sub emulator do the way Google documents the service? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 19, the emulator against the service.

choices.text: Give each subscription its own copy, `billing` only what its filter selected
choices.why: Fan-out and filters behaved as the service's.

choices.text: Forward a message to the dead-letter topic after five attempts
choices.why: With the service's own `CloudPubSubDeadLetterSource…` attributes.

choices.text: Wait 20 to 60 seconds before redelivering, as the retry policy asked
choices.why: It stored the policy and redelivered at once.

choices.text: Delete unacknowledged messages once the ten-minute retention ran out
choices.why: It enforced the bounds and deleted nothing by them.

prompt: A team creates a `fraud` subscription on `app-events`, a topic with no retention of its own, after a morning of events. What does `fraud` receive?

choices.text: Only what is published after it exists
choices.why: Right: the topic kept none of the morning's events for anybody.

choices.text: The last seven days of the topic
choices.why: Seven days is a subscription's retention of its own backlog, not the topic's history.

choices.text: The morning's events not yet acknowledged by the other subscriptions
choices.why: Each subscription keeps its own copies; nothing passes from one to another.

choices.text: Every event since the topic was created
choices.why: A topic is not a queue, and keeps nothing for a subscriber that did not exist.

prompt: On a subscription with ordering on, the reader nacks `o-102 placed` after having acknowledged nothing else of that key. On Google, what does it meet next for the key `o-102`?

choices.text: The later messages of the key first, then `o-102 placed`
choices.why: That is what the emulator did, and it is not what Google documents.

choices.text: `o-102 placed` alone, with the key paused after it
choices.why: A pause on the key is the publisher's reaction to a failed publish, not a reader's nack.

choices.text: The later messages, while `o-102 placed` goes to the dead-letter topic
choices.why: A message is dead-lettered only after the set number of attempts, five at least.

choices.text: `o-102 placed` again, followed by the later messages of the key
choices.why: Right: the message comes back together with every later one of its key, in order.

prompt: Match each way of handling a message to what a crash in the middle of it does.

pairs.right: the message is lost, in silence
the work is done again after redelivery

pairs.left: do the work and record the message's key in one transaction, then ack
pairs.right: the redelivery is refused, and the effect happens once

prompt: Quitanda's payments consumer records each message id in `processed` in the same transaction as the total. The publisher also retries a publish once. Which duplicates get through?

choices.text: The redeliveries after the consumer's crash
choices.why: Those keep their message ids, and the table refuses them.

choices.text: The upstream retry's copy, which has a fresh id
choices.why: Right: dedupe on the order id, the event's own idempotency key, to catch both.

choices.text: None; a message id identifies a payment
choices.why: Two publishes of one payment are two ids to Pub/Sub.

choices.text: Both kinds, since the table is written after the ack
choices.why: It is written with the total, before the ack, which is why redeliveries are caught.

prompt: A subscription has exactly-once delivery on. A publisher's retry puts one payment on the topic twice. What does the consumer receive?

choices.text: Both of them
choices.why: Right: two ids, one payment, both delivered; the consumer still has to dedupe.

choices.text: One message, the setting having removed the copy
choices.why: It compares no message bodies.

choices.text: One, unless the consumer is in another region
choices.why: Region changes the redelivery promise, and that promise is not about copies.

choices.text: Neither
choices.why: A topic accepts every publish; to it they are two events.

prompt: Dataflow bills batch shuffle after an adjustment: the first 250 GiB of a job at a quarter of their size, the next 4,870 GiB at half. A job shuffles 400 GiB. How many GiB are billed?
In a Beam program, Python reaches the line `parsed = lines | 'Parse' >> beam.FlatMap(parse)`. What happens at that moment?

choices.text: Every line of the input is parsed and kept in `parsed`
choices.why: The PCollection will hold the output once a runner executes the pipeline.

choices.text: A step is added to the graph, nothing more
choices.why: Right: a Beam program builds the graph first and the runner runs it after.

choices.text: The first element is parsed, to check the function works

choices.text: The step is sent to Dataflow
choices.why: The graph is handed to a runner only when the pipeline is run.

prompt: A pipeline reading a Pub/Sub subscription groups by neighbourhood with no windowing, and Beam refuses it before reading a message. Why?

choices.text: The DirectRunner cannot read Pub/Sub at all
choices.why: With a one-minute window the same runner read the subscription and gave the night's totals.

choices.text: A subscription has to be shared before it can be grouped
choices.why: A pipeline should have its own subscription; sharing would halve what it receives.

choices.text: Grouping by key is allowed only in batch
choices.why: The middle of the program ran unchanged in both; only the window was missing.

choices.text: Its global window never ends, so never emits
choices.why: Right: an unbounded collection needs a window, or a trigger that fires before the end.

prompt: A streaming job with one-minute windows has to stop for good at 19:00:40. What does draining it keep that cancelling it loses?

choices.text: The job's state, for a new version of the code to resume
choices.why: That is `--update`, which keeps the job running.

choices.text: The unacknowledged messages, which drain reads to the end of the backlog
choices.why: Drain stops reading at once.

choices.text: The totals already counted in the open minute, emitted as its window closes
choices.why: Right: drain stops reading and lets every open window close and emit.

choices.text: Nothing; both end the job the same way
choices.why: Cancel throws away windows not yet closed.

prompt: A sliding window of 30 minutes starts every 5 minutes. In how many windows is each element placed?
Fixed five-minute windows have an allowed lateness of 300 seconds. An order placed at 19:03 arrives when the watermark is at 19:12. What happens to it?

choices.text: It is emitted in a `LATE` pane of the 19:00 window
choices.why: That needs the watermark to be before 19:10, the window's end plus the lateness.

choices.text: Dropped, with no error: the window's state went at 19:10
choices.why: Right: lateness is measured against the watermark, and nothing reports the loss.

choices.text: It is moved into the 19:10 window, the one now open
choices.why: An element belongs to the window of its event time, or to none.

choices.text: The pipeline fails with an error naming the order
choices.why: No step fails and no error is logged for dropped late data.

prompt: A pipeline emits early panes and writes each one as a row per window and neighbourhood, overwriting the row each time. Which accumulation mode does that sink need?

choices.text: Discarding, so that each pane is only what arrived since the last
choices.why: Overwriting with a part would leave the row holding only the last part.

choices.text: Either, since the on-time pane repairs the row
choices.why: In discarding mode the on-time pane can be 0.00, and the row would say so.

choices.text: Neither; early panes cannot be written to a table
choices.why: A row per window in a table is the lesson's own example of such a sink.

choices.text: Accumulating, so that every pane is the whole window so far
choices.why: Right: the last pane written is the answer, and a pane delivered twice does no harm.

prompt: Sessions have a gap of five minutes. Customer `c-30` orders at 20:00:00 and at 20:04:30, and not again that evening. What session does the pipeline make?

choices.why: Right: the orders are under five minutes apart, and a session ends at the last one plus the gap.
The session runs on past the last element by the gap.

choices.text: Two, one for each order
choices.why: They would be two only if more than five minutes apart.

choices.text: One, from 20:00:00 to 20:05:00, aligned to the clock
choices.why: Alignment to the clock is what fixed windows do; a session is made from the data.

prompt: Dataproc's management fee is 0.010 USD per vCPU-hour, on every vCPU of the master and of both kinds of worker. A cluster has a master and 10 workers, all `n2-standard-4` (4 vCPU). What is the fee for one hour, in USD?
A Dataproc cluster is to run a large nightly batch cheaply on Spot VMs. Which machines can be Spot without risking more than time?

choices.text: The primary workers, as Dataproc rebalances their blocks

choices.text: The master, which only coordinates
choices.why: Losing the master ends the cluster.

choices.text: The secondary workers, since they hold no HDFS
choices.why: Right: a lost secondary's tasks are run again elsewhere; nothing is lost but time.

choices.text: Every machine, with a high-availability master
choices.why: HA protects the master; the primaries still hold HDFS.

prompt: A cluster that runs for weeks has secondary workers. Why choose Spot rather than preemptible for them?

choices.why: They are spare capacity and are reclaimed when Google needs it.

choices.text: Spot VMs may hold HDFS blocks, and preemptible ones may not
choices.why: Neither secondary type holds HDFS; that is what makes them secondary.

choices.text: Preemptible VMs stop within 24 hours; Spot do not
choices.why: Right: both can be taken back with about thirty seconds' warning, but only one has a daily end.

choices.text: Preemptible VMs cost the same as standard ones
choices.why: Both are sold below the standard price.

prompt: A Composer 2 small environment pays an environment fee of 0.56 USD an hour, on top of its components. What is that fee alone in a 730-hour month, in USD to the cent?

prompt: A Datastream stream was deleted and its PostgreSQL replication slot left behind. What happens on the source over the next weeks?

choices.why: PostgreSQL keeps a slot until somebody drops it.

choices.text: The slot holds the log from its bookmark onward, and the disk fills
choices.why: Right: drop a slot when its reader is gone, or cap it with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`.

choices.text: Writes are refused until a reader connects to the slot
choices.why: Writes go on; it is the retained log that grows.

choices.text: Datastream is billed for the changes the slot keeps
choices.why: Datastream bills what it processes, and nothing for an idle stream.

prompt: On a PostgreSQL slot, a reader calls `pg_logical_slot_peek_changes` and then `pg_logical_slot_get_changes`. What does a second `get` straight after return?

choices.text: Nothing, because `get` moved the slot's bookmark past those changes
choices.why: Right: `peek` reads and leaves; `get` reads and moves the bookmark.

choices.text: The same changes again, as `get` and `peek` both leave them
choices.why: Only `peek` leaves them.

choices.text: The changes `peek` read, since `peek` reserved them for the next call
choices.why: `peek` reserves nothing; it moves no bookmark at all.

choices.text: An error, as a slot can be read once
choices.why: It can be read any number of times; it simply has nothing left.

prompt: Quitanda puts its raw bucket into a raw zone of the `sales` lake, and grants the analysts only the curated zone. A colleague still has `storage.objects.get` on the raw bucket through IAM. Can she read it?

prompt: A Dataplex quality rule says `phone` is not null, with a threshold of 95%. Tonight's 20 orders include one with no phone. What does the rule report?

prompt: `phone` in the curated orders carries a policy tag, and the analysts do not hold Fine-Grained Reader on it. What happens when an analyst runs `SELECT order_id, phone FROM quitanda.orders`?
